parsed_answer.content: The SOLID principles represent five foundational pillars of Object-Oriented Programming and design, conceptualized by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob). These principles—Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion—serve as architectural guardrails designed to combat software rot, brittleness, and rigid codebases. When applied correctly in a strongly-typed, class-based language like Java, they enforce high cohesion and loose coupling. High cohesion ensures that a class or module focuses on a single, well-defined domain concept, while loose coupling minimizes direct dependencies between distinct system layers, making the architecture resilient to requirement changes, easy to unit test, and straightforward to refactor without triggering cascading failures.

items: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. By restricting a class to a single actor or business capability, we limit the impact radius of future modifications.

Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. We achieve this via polymorphism, abstract classes, and interfaces, allowing new behavior to be plugged in without rewriting legacy code.

Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. Overriding methods with empty bodies, throwing unexpected UnsupportedOperationExceptions, or weakening preconditions violates this.
Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use. Fat interfaces should be split into fine-grained, role-specific contracts.

Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Furthermore, abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.

parsed_answer.content: A common production anti-pattern is blindly applying SRP to the point of class explosion, creating dozens of micro-classes that obfuscate business logic rather than clarifying it. Use domain-driven design (DDD) boundaries and common-sense cohesion metrics to balance SRP with practical maintainability. Additionally, watch out for LSP violations when using inheritance for code reuse instead of true behavioral subtyping.
